# Data Analytics {#sec-analytics}

This section covers all analytical methods applied to the prepared data:
descriptive spatial analytics, predictive modelling of demand (SVM and
neural networks), and reinforcement learning for smart charging.

## Descriptive (Spatial) Analytics {#sec-eda}
To better understand the characteristics of taxi demand before developing predictive models, we first perform a descriptive analysis of the dataset. The analysis investigates spatial and temporal demand patterns, examines trip characteristics, compares different spatial aggregation levels, and identifies persistent demand hot spots. 
### Demand Patterns
The taxi demand data exhibit strong spatial and temporal heterogeneity. Most trips are relatively short in terms of both travel distance and duration, while trip fares show a pronounced right-skewed distribution. Consequently, the majority of journeys are inexpensive, whereas a comparatively small number of long-distance trips account for substantially higher fares.
Spatially, taxi activity is highly concentrated in a limited number of locations. Pickup and dropoff demand are strongly correlated, indicating that areas generating many departures also receive many arrivals. However, comparing pickup and dropoff distributions reveals localized differences that likely reflect commuting flows, airport traffic, and the separation of residential and commercial districts.
Additional descriptive statistics and distribution plots are provided in **Appendix A**.

### Spatial Patterns
Taxi demand was analysed using community areas, census tracts and H3 hexagonal grids at multiple resolutions. Although all representations reveal similar large-scale demand structures, the selected spatial resolution considerably influences the observed level of detail.
Community areas provide a coarse overview of demand, while census tracts capture substantially finer local variation. H3 resolution 7 offers a compromise between spatial detail and robustness, whereas H3 resolution 8 largely reproduces the census tract representation. This behaviour results from the privacy-preserving coordinate masking applied to the original dataset, where published coordinates correspond to census tract centroids whenever available.
**[Figure X: Spatial demand distribution]**
Across all spatial resolutions, demand remains highly concentrated in only a small number of regions. Increasing spatial resolution improves the visibility of localized demand patterns but simultaneously introduces considerable sparsity, with many spatial units containing few or no observations during large parts of the observation period.
Further spatial comparisons, concentration measures, Lorenz curves and pickup-dropoff difference maps are shown in **Appendix A**.

### Temporal Patterns
Taxi demand follows clear and recurring temporal patterns. Demand is lowest during the early morning hours, increases throughout the day and reaches pronounced peaks during commuting and evening leisure periods. Distinct differences are also observed between weekdays and weekends, reflecting changes in travel behaviour.
**[Figure X: Average hourly taxi demand]**
Besides the intraday cycle, demand also varies systematically across weekdays and seasons, indicating that temporal information is highly informative for subsequent forecasting models.
Additional temporal analyses, including weekday-weekend comparisons and seasonal demand patterns, are provided in **Appendix A**.

### Demand Hot Spots
Persistent demand hot spots were identified using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) and Kernel Density Estimation (KDE). Both approaches consistently identify the central business district and major transportation hubs as the dominant centres of taxi activity.
**[Figure X: Gaussian Mixture Model hot spots]**
The probabilistic clustering produced by the GMM groups regions with similar spatial demand characteristics, while KDE provides a continuous representation of demand intensity. Both methods highlight areas associated with dense commercial activity, transportation infrastructure and entertainment facilities, demonstrating the strong influence of land use on taxi demand.
The complementary KDE visualisation is presented in **Appendix A**.

## Predictive Analytics (SVM & Neural Networks) {#sec-prediction}

Fleet planning needs to know where and when demand will appear before a shift
starts. We predict trip starts per spatial unit and time bucket from the cell's
identity and location, calendar, weather, and POI features alone, a scenario
question such as expected demand on a rainy Sunday morning on the outskirts, not
an extrapolation from the previous hour. Two model families are compared: a
Support Vector Machine, fitted directly on demand and on the residual over a
historical-mean baseline, and a feedforward neural network. Both train across
six grids crossing three spatial units (H3 resolution 7, census tract, community
area) with hourly and daily bins, and both are scored against the same
historical-mean baseline, letting us ask whether a learned model, and a deep one
especially, earns its added complexity.

The target is `Total_Trip_Start`, the trip count per spatial unit and time
bucket. The three spatial units carry 108 active hexagons at H3 resolution 7,
496 active census tracts, and 77 community areas, after dropping inactive units
with no pickups in the observation window during grid construction
(@sec-data-prep). Sparsity differs sharply: zero-demand rows range from 0.8% at
community/daily to 96.5% at census/hourly, driving the sampling decisions taken
separately for each model family below.

The reference point throughout is a historical mean per spatial unit, keyed by
month and day of week, plus hour on the hourly grids. Computed on the training
split alone and merged into validation and test, it carries no future
information and serves double duty: as the `base_demand` feature available to
both models, and as the skill-score benchmark, `1 - MAE_model / MAE_baseline`.
Skill rather than raw MAE is reported because mean demand differs by roughly a
factor of 80 across the six grids, making raw errors incomparable between them.

Train, validation, and test are cut along the calendar rather than drawn at
random: the earliest 50% of unique dates train the models (2024-01-01 to
2025-03-06), the next 20% validate (2025-03-07 to 2025-08-26), and the final 30%
are held out for testing (2025-08-27 to 2026-05-12). A random row-level split
would leak autocorrelated demand into the test set and contaminate
`base_demand`. Model selection runs on validation; test is scored once, for the
selected models.

### Support Vector Machine

<!-- Source notebooks: notebooks/3.2 PredictionCommonGround.ipynb (shared
registry, sampling, scoring), 3.2a PredictionSVMStandard.ipynb (direct),
3.2b PredictionSVMResidual.ipynb (residual). Validation figures below are read
from the post-zero-mile-drop artifacts in models_predictions/SVR/. -->

Two SVR models train on identical splits, samples, and candidate feature sets,
differing only in the prediction target. The direct model regresses
`log1p(Total_Trip_Start)` and converts predictions back with `expm1`, clipped at
zero. The residual model instead predicts the log-space correction to the
historical mean, `log1p(demand) - log1p(base_demand)`, and reconstructs counts as
`expm1(log1p(base_demand) + correction_hat)`; it never sees the raw target, only
how far a cell and time bucket departs from its own history. The reasoning:
`base_demand` already carries much of the predictable signal, so a model
reproducing it from scratch would spend capacity re-deriving what the pipeline
already computed. Because the correction sits on a far smaller scale and variance
than `log1p(demand)`, hyperparameters tuned for one target do not transfer to the
other, so each is tuned separately.

SVR's fit cost is quadratic in sample size, so each level trains on a
class-balanced sample: all non-zero training rows plus an equal number of zero
rows (4,000 for the kernel scan, 8,000 for the grid search, the winner then
re-scored on a 50,000-row validation draw). Levels with little zero demand, such
as community/daily at 0.8%, end up non-zero-heavy instead. A uniform sample of
the same size would be 94% empty at h3_7/hourly and 96.5% at census/hourly,
leaving little for a model to learn beyond predicting zero. Validation and test
stay unbalanced, so both models are scored at a natural prevalence they never
trained on.

Tuning runs in two stages per level and feature set: a kernel scan compares
linear, polynomial, and RBF at a fixed baseline setting, judged by validation R²
in count space, and the winning kernel alone carries into a three-fold grid
search over `C` and `gamma` (extended by `degree` where polynomial wins), scored
by count-space MAE. Four feature sets compete at every level: a basic
calendar/location/history block, plus weather, plus POI, plus both.
@tbl-svr-search-grid lists every searched value and sample size;
@tbl-svr-feature-blocks lists the four feature blocks.

#### Validation Results
The direct model does not beat the historical mean feature it is given. At five
of six levels its tuned winner trails the baseline on validation MAE, from -3.5%
at community/daily to -35.5% at census/hourly, and the one level it wins,
h3_7/daily, it wins by just 0.2%. Predicting the correction instead lifts the
skill score at all six levels, though unevenly: community/daily is the one clear
win, at +5.3% (R² = 0.970); h3_7/daily turns its tie into a slim +1.2%;
h3_7/hourly and census/daily stay near ties at +0.3%; community/hourly remains
just short of the baseline at -1.0%. Census/hourly, the sparsest grid at 96.5%
zero rows, loses heavily under both strategies (-35.5% direct, -32.1% residual),
with MAE skill deeply negative while RMSE skill stays roughly flat (+0.7%
residual). Daily aggregation beats hourly at all three spatial resolutions under
both strategies, since hourly bins are sparser and noisier.

Every winning direct model needs the flexible RBF kernel; four of the six
winning residual models do just as well with a straight line (both h3_7 levels,
census/hourly, and community/daily). Both models operate on a compressed scale
that gets expanded back into trip counts, so a small error before expansion
becomes large after it. The direct model predicts demand itself, anywhere from
zero to several thousand trips a day, and needs the extra curvature to stop those
errors from compounding; the residual model predicts only a small adjustment, so
even a straight line stays close enough that expansion cannot run away with it.
All six residual winners settle at `C=1`, against direct winners spread from
`C=1` to `C=50`.

The two best models are both residual. At community/daily, a linear fit at `C=1`
on the basic+weather feature set brings the average error down from the
baseline's 36.19 trips per area-day to 34.25, at R² = 0.970. Second is
h3_7/daily, on the basic+poi feature set, also linear at `C=1`, moving 15.83
trips per hexagon-day to 15.64 at R² = 0.954. Both sit on daily grids, correct a
historical mean rather than predicting demand outright, and need no curved
kernel. The operational margin is small: roughly two trips per area per day at
the better of the two, and about a fifth of a trip per hexagon at the other.

### Deep Learning Model {#sec-nn}

<!-- Source notebook: notebooks/3.3 PredictionDeepLearning_Res7.ipynb -->
<!-- TODO: Feedforward NN architecture, training setup, results per resolution. -->

For the neural network, we used a feedforward network that predicts 
log1p-transformed trip counts, which are then back-transformed via expm1 
for evaluation. We trained on the full training split without any 
zero/non-zero balancing, since our experiments showed that balanced sampling 
actually hurt the FNN's performance. For all six levels we used the same 
feature set, combining basic temporal and location features with all 14 POI 
categories and 5 weather variables. We did not test different feature set 
combinations as we did for the SVM, mostly due to computational constraints. 
The network uses ReLU activations in the hidden layers, a linear output unit, 
MSE as the loss function, and AdamW with a weight decay of 1e-4. Training ran 
for up to 15 epochs with a batch size of 250. Within each training run, we 
used early stopping with a patience of 3 to select the best checkpoint based 
on validation loss, preventing the model from training past its best point. 
To find the best architecture per level, we ran a grid search over four layer 
configurations ([64,32,16], [128,64,32], [128,64,32,16], [256,128,64,32]), 
three learning rates (0.01, 0.001, 0.0001), and two dropout rates (0.0, 0.2), 
giving 24 configurations per level. The winning configuration per level was 
selected by validation MAE in count space. The final performance of each 
winning model was then evaluated once on the held-out test set, with results 
reported in (Figure X) across MAE, RMSE and R². Looking at these 
results, h3_7/hourly comes out as the best performing level overall. As shown
in (Table X), smaller and shallower networks worked best for the 
denser levels like h3_7/hourly and community, while census levels needed 
deeper networks and lower learning rates. Census/daily was the only level 
where dropout helped, which fits with it being the hardest level to train 
given its very high share of zero-demand rows. 
(Table X)shows the FNN results across all six spatial-temporal levels.
The model beats the historical-mean baseline at four of the six levels, with
h3_7/hourly performing best at a skill score of +6.3% MAE. The gains are
small across all levels. Two levels perform notably worse: census/hourly is
essentially a coin flip at -0.1%, and census/daily loses to the baseline by
a large margin (-20.3% MAE, -44.7% RMSE). These are the two sparsest and most
zero-inflated levels in our dataset, and the SVM struggles there as well,
which suggests the difficulty lies in the data rather than the model choice.
Overall, the FNN performs best at finer temporal resolution and denser spatial
units, while coarser and sparser levels remain hard to predict beyond a simple
historical average. (Check after training)

### Model Comparison

Both models types are compared on the same held-out test split, at H3 resolution 7
and at both temporal bins, against the same historical-mean baseline. Census and
community levels are excluded: [GAP]the SVM was scored there, but no matching neural
network prediction file exists, so a comparison at those levels would not be
like-for-like. The comparison runs along six lines, each asking a different
question about where a model's error actually falls. Supporting figures and
tables are collected in @sec-appendix.

- **Aggregate accuracy.** MAE, RMSE and R² for the baseline, the SVM and the
  network at each temporal resolution, establishing whether either model beats
  the historical mean at all and by how much (@tbl-svm-vs-nn-overall).
- **Predicted against actual.** Predicted versus observed demand per cell and
  bucket, which exposes systematic over- or under-prediction and the demand range
  at which the fit degrades, read as spread away from the diagonal
  (@fig-svm-vs-nn-scatter).
- **Spatial error.** Error aggregated per hexagon and mapped three ways: absolute
  error (@fig-svm-hex-mae), error relative to each cell's own mean demand
  (@fig-svm-hex-mre), and the share of each cell's day-to-day variation the model
  explains (@fig-svm-hex-r2). The absolute and relative views answer different
  questions, since the largest absolute errors concentrate downtown purely because
  demand is largest there, while the relative view is what makes the quiet outer
  cells legible at all.
- **Head-to-head by location.** The per-hexagon difference `MAE_NN - MAE_SVM`
  mapped directly, so that which model wins where is read off a single diverging
  scale rather than inferred by comparing two separate colour ramps
  (@fig-svm-vs-nn-hex-delta).
- **Temporal error.** Error by day of week (@fig-svm-vs-nn-dayofweek,
  @fig-svm-vs-nn-dayofweek-relerr) and, on the hourly grid only, by hour of day
  (@fig-svm-vs-nn-hourofday, @fig-svm-vs-nn-hourofday-relerr), each in absolute
  terms and relative to mean demand. This separates error that simply tracks
  demand volume from error concentrated at particular times, such as the overnight
  hours where demand is near zero and small absolute misses dominate the relative
  figure. City-wide predicted and actual demand across the full test period is
  plotted alongside as a sanity check on aggregate level and drift
  (@fig-svm-vs-nn-timeseries).
- **Error by segment.** Test MAE, relative error and skill score broken down by
  demand band (zero, 1-10, 11-100, and above 100 trips) and by weather (dry
  against rainy days), as a table (@tbl-svm-vs-nn-segments) and as relative error
  per segment (@fig-svm-vs-nn-segments-relerr). This is the decisive view for
  fleet planning, because a model that wins on average can still lose on exactly
  the busiest cells, or on the rainy days, that matter operationally.

### Shortfalls and Improvement Levers {#sec-shortfalls}

<!-- Sources: docs/report_content_guide.md 4.2 "Shortfalls & improvement levers".
NOTE on the two-stage-search check: the full per-kernel run in
models_predictions/SVR/residual_kernelgrid/ dates from 23 Jul, before the
zero-mile-trip drop (its h3_7/daily baseline val MAE is 14.658 vs. 15.830 in the
current run), so its skill figures are not comparable to the reported ones. The
claim is therefore kept qualitative -- do not quote cross-run numbers from it
without re-running that search on the post-drop data. -->

Neither family clears the historical mean by a wide margin, and the reasons split
into three groups: limits specific to the SVM, limits specific to the network, and
limits the two share.

For the support vector machine, one failure mode is specific and fixable. The
residual model is worse than the baseline precisely on cells whose demand turns
out to be zero, because the correction term does not shrink to zero where it
should, and zero rows dominate most levels. A floor on the reconstructed
correction, or a gate that decides zero against non-zero before regressing
magnitude, would both be worth testing. Smaller gains could come from rebalancing
the sample (a natural-prevalence draw performed worse) or from a larger one,
though SVR's quadratic fit cost is what forced a balanced subsample in the first
place, so more rows trade directly against the breadth of the tuning search.

The **network's** limits are ones of search breadth rather than a diagnosed
failure. A single feature set was used at every level, so unlike the SVM there is
no evidence on whether weather or POI features help or hurt the network at any
given level; repeating the four-way feature-set comparison is the most direct
improvement lever. The architecture search was bounded the same way, covering
layer width, learning rate and dropout across 24 configurations while holding
batch size, activation function and epoch budget fixed. No permutation-importance
or comparable interpretability check was run for the network, only for the direct
SVR, so whether the weather and POI blocks contribute at all is currently unknown.

**Both** families fail on the same grids. Census/hourly and census/daily, the
sparsest and most zero-inflated levels, defeat each of them, which points at the
data rather than at either model choice. More generally, `base_demand` already
carries most of the signal that a scenario-conditioned framing makes available, so
both models compete for a thin margin on top of an already strong baseline. The
levers that would widen that margin are therefore shared: weather interacted with
hour and location rather than entered additively, weather resolved spatially
instead of drawn from a single citywide coordinate (@sec-data-prep), and POI
expressed as distances to the nearest attractor rather than as counts inside the
cell.

### Executive Summary
An automated charging controller was designed and evaluated for the client's ride-hailing EV fleet, comparing two reinforcement learning methods: Tabular Q-Learning and a Deep Q-Network (DQN). Across five independent training runs, Tabular Q-Learning reduced the average daily charging cost by roughly 22% relative to a naive always-full-power baseline, with the probability of running out of energy remaining close to that baseline. DQN achieved comparable average performance with fewer training episodes but showed substantially higher variability across runs and is not recommended for deployment at this stage. The DQN approach may become more relevant as for example the state complexity increases greatly.

### Problem Framing & Methodology
Each vehicle returns home at 2:00 PM and must depart at 4:00 PM. During this window, an automated controller decides every 15 minutes how fast to charge the battery, choosing from four charging speeds. Electricity prices rise later in the afternoon, while the energy required for the day's shift is unknown until departure and varies around 30 kWh. Running out of energy mid-shift causes a missed fare and a stranded vehicle is substantially more costly than a marginally higher electricity bill. Thus, the controller must balance cost against this risk.
The problem was formalized as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). At each step, the model observes battery level and remaining time, and selects one of four charging speeds (0, 7.33, 14.67, or 22 kW). Each decision incurs a small electricity cost, and a $500 penalty applies if the battery is insufficient at departure. This penalty was set far above the maximum achievable savings from smart charging (at most a few cents per day) so that the model always prioritizes reliability. The arrival battery level is drawn from a uniform distribution (0–50% of capacity) rather than assumed as always empty, reflecting realistic driver behavior and creating a genuine cost-risk trade-off. The per-kWh price coefficient rises from ~7 to ~11 cents across the eight time steps, incentivizing earlier charging where safe.
Two methods were compared: Tabular Q-Learning, a lookup table well suited to this problem's small, enumerable state space, and DQN, which replaces the table with a neural network capable of generalizing across states. Each method was trained independently five times with different random seeds and evaluated on several thousand simulated days per run, to avoid drawing conclusions from a single, potentially lucky training outcome.

### Results

#### Tabular Q-Learning
Training over 150,000 simulated days shows the training score improving and then stabilizing, with the failure rate dropping sharply to a low, stable level (@fig-learning_curve, @fig-failure_rate_curve), indicating convergence to a consistent policy. The learned policy (@fig-policy_heatmap_verified) uses both intermediate charging speeds across a substantial share of states rather than only the extremes, indicating a genuinely differentiated strategy.
Tabular Q-Learning reduced the average daily cost from $1.92 to $1.50 ± $0.02 while keeping the failure probability (0.11% ± 0.09%) close to the naive baseline (@tbl-naive-qtabular). Overall, a roughly 22% cost reduction without a measurable increase in stranded-vehicle risk.

#### Deep Q-Network
DQN's training curves (@fig-learning_curve_dqn, @fig-failure_curve_dqn) oscillate throughout the full 20,000-episode period rather than stabilizing, so the best-performing weights observed at any point were retained rather than the final ones. Increasing episodes further did not help, which is also why DQN required far fewer episodes than the tabular approach (20,000 vs. 150,000), reducing the compute time needed drastically.
The retained policy (@fig-dqn_policy_heatmap) charges at full power in almost all states, differing from the naive baseline in only two narrow state regions. Largely reproducing the naive strategy rather than a materially different one. The DQN heatmap appears fully populated while the Q-table heatmap only covers a diagonal band, because the Q-table stores entries only for visited states, whereas the neural network returns an output for any input, including states never encountered during training.
DQN reduced the average daily cost to $1.46 ± $0.24 with a failure probability of 1.16% ± 0.96% which is comparable on average to Tabular Q-Learning, but with much greater variability across runs (@tbl-dqn-summary). The per-seed variation is one of the key findings: one run reproduced the naive strategy almost exactly, while the other four achieved lower costs at markedly higher failure rates (@tbl-dqn-breakdown). This inconsistency, more than the average result, is why DQN is not recommended for production use at this stage, as we are able to achieve comparable or even better results with noticeably less effort.
